result:
The proposed answer of 7 is not supported. The argument is largely heuristic, and its key n=6 example fails.

**What checks out:**
- **n=4:** The single 4-edge {1,2,3,4} covers all four triples but has only one edge, so it has no Berge-C_4^3. Hence n₀ > 4.
- **n=5:** Take the 4-edge E = {1,2,3,4} plus 3-edges covering every triple containing 5. In any 5-cycle, vertex 5 lies in exactly 3 of the 5 consecutive windows, so 2 windows avoid 5. Both must be covered by E, which can be used only once. So there is no Berge-C_5^3, and n₀ > 5.

**Where the proposed solution fails:**
- **n=6:** The proposed construction, E₁={1,2,3,4}, E₂={1,2,5,6}, E₃={3,4,5,6} plus 3-edges, does contain a Berge-C_6^3. Label the pairs A={1,2}, B={3,4}, C={5,6}. The cyclic order 1,3,5,2,4,6 gives six windows {1,3,5}, {3,5,2}, {5,2,4}, {2,4,6}, {4,6,1}, {6,1,3}. Each is a transversal triple, and each is a 3-edge. These six distinct 3-edges form a Berge-C_6^3, so this is not a counterexample.
- I also checked the other natural covers of all triples by 4-edges, including the minimum 6-edge cover (the complements of two disjoint triangles) and a 7-edge variant. Each contains a Berge-C_6^3. I did not find a 6-vertex counterexample, so the proposed claim that n=6 fails is unsupported.
- **n=7:** The argument relies on a Steiner system S(3,4,7), which is irrelevant to whether a counterexample exists. The assertion that "any hypergraph on n ≥ 7 vertices … will inevitably" work is not justified.

So the verified lower bound is n₀ ≥ 6, not 7. The true value appears to be 6 unless a subtler 6-vertex counterexample exists, which I could not find. I did not exhaustively check all 6-vertex hypergraphs or the case n ≥ 7, so I cannot confirm the exact value.

VERDICT: REJECT
CONFIDENCE: 2
